title: Leveling the Playing Field -- Ch. 19: Velarde v. Social Justice Party: Form and Substance of Judicial Decisions
keywords: for the guidance of the bench and the bar
primary_topics: Chapter 19 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' -- CJP's account of Velarde v. Social Justice Party, the Decision he himself wrote, in which the Supreme Court found it impossible to rule on whether religious leaders may endorse candidates because the trial court's 'Decision' failed the form and substance required by the Constitution

The procedural collapse of the SJS Petition for Declaratory Relief: no justiciable controversy, no ultimate facts, no cause of action and no legal standing, so that the suit sought only a forbidden advisory opinion

The catalogue of irregularities in the Regional Trial Court -- unheard Motions to Dismiss, an unreasoned Order, unresolved Motions for Reconsideration, and a 'Decision' issued before answers were filed -- amounting to inexplicable haste and grave abuse of discretion

The Court's extended guidance, given 'for the guidance of the bench and the bar,' on the five essential parts of a good decision: statement of the case, statement of facts, issues, the court's ruling and the dispositive portion
sub_topics: The framing question: do religious leaders violate the separation of Church and State when they endorse candidates or urge their flock to vote for particular candidates?

The facts: on January 28, 2003 the Social Justice Society filed a Petition for Declaratory Relief in RTC-Manila Branch 49 against Brother Mike Velarde, Jaime Cardinal Sin, Eraño Manalo, Eddie Villanueva and Eli Soriano, and won a favorable 'Decision' on June 12, 2003
On appeal the Supreme Court treated the question as transcendental and novel, gave it priority and held Oral Argument on April 13, 2004 on procedural and substantive issues

Justiciable controversy: the SJS Petition alleged no existing dispute, no specific violated right and no ultimate facts, resting instead on speculation that the religious leaders had endorsed or threatened to endorse candidates
Because the Petition merely asked the trial court's opinion on a speculated endorsement, it sought an advisory opinion, which courts are proscribed from rendering

Cause of action: in declaratory relief no actual breach is presupposed, but a breach must be impending, imminent or at least threatened, and the party must show direct injury rather than an indefinite grievance
SJS alleged no legal right of its own; its claimed interest in a judicial clarification was impersonal, vague, highly speculative and not material to the issue
During Oral Argument Velarde and his co-respondents all strongly asserted that they had never engaged or intended to engage in partisan politics

Legal standing: no illegal disbursement of taxpayers' money and no showing of adverse effect -- though the Court noted standing could be waived given an issue transcendental in importance and novel in nature

The trial court's irregularities: it did not hear the Motions to Dismiss, gave no reason for denying them, failed to resolve the Motions for Reconsideration, and decided without allowing the parties to answer

The constitutional command that no decision be rendered without expressing clearly and distinctly the facts and the law on which it is based -- violated by an assailed Decision with no statement of facts and no final disposition
The rejection of the claim that a sentence on page 10 was the dispositive portion, citing Magdalena Estate, Inc. v. Caluag that the dispositive portion prevails over the opinion

The Court's template for a good decision: statement of the case, statement of facts (objective, synthesis, subjective or combined methods), issues or assignment of errors, the court's ruling, and the disposition, with an optional prologue and epilogue

The four-part test of completeness of a disposition -- the parties know their rights and obligations, know how to execute under alternative contingencies, need no further proceedings, and the case terminates according to the proper relief
The style prescription: language fresh and free-flowing, not stereotyped, 'much less highfalutin, hackneyed and pretentious,' and always clear, concise, complete and correct
The outcome: because the assailed Decision made no findings of fact and no final disposition, it was void and legally inexistent, leaving nothing for the Court to review, affirm, reverse or modify

stances.claim: The transcendental question whether religious leaders may endorse candidates could not be decided, because the SJS Petition alleged no existing controversy, no ultimate facts and no violated right, and therefore asked the courts for a forbidden advisory opinion on a merely speculated endorsement.
stances.rhetorical_move: justiciability gatekeeping: testing the pleading against the requirements of an actual case before touching the constitutional merits

stances.claim: A judgment that contains no statement of facts and no final resolution of the petition violates the constitutional command to express clearly and distinctly the facts and the law on which it is based, and is therefore void and legally inexistent, leaving nothing on appeal to review, affirm, reverse or modify.
stances.rhetorical_move: constitutional form-and-substance test applied to the lower court's own writing, with the nullity following as a consequence

stances.claim: Trial courts must follow the elementary procedure of hearing motions, stating the grounds of their orders, resolving motions for reconsideration and allowing answers before deciding; departing from it, as the RTC did, is inexplicable haste and grave abuse of discretion that wastes precious judicial time and effort.
stances.rhetorical_move: corrective instruction 'for the guidance of the bench and the bar,' converting a single lapse into a general template

notable_anecdotes: CJP notes that he personally wrote the Court's ruling in Velarde v. Social Justice Party, and frames the chapter as his own explanation of a case he had 'the honor of writing.'

He recounts that the Court considered the question transcendental enough to hold Oral Argument on April 13, 2004 and give the case priority -- only to find, after deliberating, that no decision on the merits was possible.
At the Oral Argument, Velarde and his co-respondents firmly assured the Court that they had done nothing to trigger the issue and had never intended to participate in partisan politics.

He reproduces the Court's rejection of the claim that the dispositive portion of the 14-page RTC Decision lay in a single sentence on page 10, invoking Magdalena Estate to hold that an opinion 'ordering nothing' cannot supply the deficiency.

Because of its importance he quotes at length the Court's own primer on what a good decision must contain, down to the reminder that an epilogue 'may also lay down an enduring philosophy of law or guiding principle.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 19 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' explained Velarde v. Social Justice Party, the Decision CJP himself wrote, which arose from the Social Justice Society's Petition for Declaratory Relief asking whether religious leaders violate the separation of Church and State by endorsing candidates or urging their flock to vote for particular ones. The Regional Trial Court of Manila had ruled for SJS on June 12, 2003, and the Supreme Court, thinking the question transcendental and novel, gave the appeal priority and held Oral Argument on April 13, 2004 -- only to conclude that no decision on the merits was possible. The Petition, he recounted, alleged no existing controversy between the parties, no specific violated right and no ultimate facts; it rested on the speculation that Brother Mike Velarde and his co-respondents had endorsed or threatened to endorse candidates, and so sought only an advisory opinion, which courts are proscribed from rendering. It likewise stated no cause of action, since no breach was impending or threatened and no direct injury was shown, and SJS lacked legal standing, its claimed 'keen interest' being impersonal, vague and highly speculative -- though the Court observed that standing could be waived for an issue of paramount public interest. The proceedings below were tainted as well: the trial court did not hear the Motions to Dismiss, gave no reason for denying them, left the Motions for Reconsideration unresolved, and decided before answers were filed, acting with inexplicable haste and grave abuse of discretion. Because the assailed Decision contained no statement of facts and no final disposition, it violated the constitutional command that decisions express clearly and distinctly the facts and the law on which they rest, and was void and legally inexistent, leaving nothing to review. For the guidance of the bench and the bar, CJP then reproduced the Court's primer on the five essential parts of a good decision, closing with the standard that a decision be clear, concise, complete and correct.
